utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I suppose this is properly described as a 65 ter meeting. If we need a designation for it, that should make it clear to all concerned that although it's taking place in private, in camera, that as before, the transcript will, if it seems appropriate, be made public. The first thing, I think, to do is to record who is present. I note that Mr. Karadzic is present, as he has been at any such meetings, but I'm delighted to see that he is not on his own this time. I won't express too high a degree of pleasure at that, just at the moment, but I think it's a very useful exercise on this occasion to have the assistance of at least one of his assigned associates, and I take it you are Mr. Sladojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I'm pleased to meet you. Can I now have confirmation of who is here for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, Julian Nicholls, trial attorney, and myself, Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Retzlaff. I have ask the Registry in the form of someone from OLAD at least should be here, and we have Ms. Reinhardt in that capacity. Now, I want at the outset to make one thing very clear to avoid any misunderstanding. And that is that I don't have power, nor does a Trial Chamber as an entity have power to tell OLAD what to do or the Registry what to do in the context of this sort of meeting. Obviously there are circumstances in which the Trial Chamber may be asked to make determinations which do affect the work of the Registry. So my role in this meeting, which is for a fairly limited purpose, is to try to facilitate agreement on matters, insofar as there can be agreement. I anticipate, however, that we will not leave here with clear agreement on how matters affecting all the expert witnesses that are at issue today are to be resolved from here on in. But let's see how far we can go. And the first issue I would like to address is the question of, I think, broadly is best described as the issue of DNA. It was when I saw the exchanges of correspondence about this that I thought that it was worth having this meeting to make sure that there are no misunderstandings about where we are going on this. Now, I think the best plan, Mr. Sladojevic, if you don't mind, is for you, if you are willing to do so, and Mr. Karadzic is happy that you should do so, if you could explain to me exactly what it is you have requested is provided to you, and the reason for that in as simple terms as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if I may I suggest that I explain at least how I understand the whole problem with the ICMP and the pathology reports that we need. There are a couple of steps the Defence has to undertake in order to establish basically what happened in Srebrenica and other crime bases. So basically the evidence that in Srebrenica had been killed or died so many people are the DNA reports on the one hand, and on the other hand, pathology reports or exhumation reports on the other hand. The first one serves to establish the identity of the victim, and the other one to establish the causes and mechanisms or reasons of that, origin of that. So our position is to ask basically, was to ask the Prosecution and ICMP through the Prosecution to disclose all relevant documents that are related to the identification of victims, and because of the very limited resources that we have at our disposal, we suggested to analyse about 5 per cent out of approximately 6.000 allegedly done identification cases, which is around 300 cases that the ICMP basically did. And then on the basis of this analysis, to give our assessment or the -- to give his assessment of the validity or accuracy of the procedure. Now the -- our expert explained that he needs 300 cases for the following reasons, because the Prosecution expert, Dr. Parsons, he said that the procedure of establishing identity of victims has evolved over time since 2002. So that's around last -- it concerns the six years, so we suggested then 50 cases for each year, which makes 300. Now, that is only one side of the problem that we have. The other side of the problem luckily for me was explained to greater detail by the forensic expert Dr. Dunjic, and so he sent a memorandum or a letter explaining the problem in greater detail. So if you don't mind, I can -- unfortunately we have it only in Serbian version, in Serbian language, and since we got it last night, and if you would like, I could give you -- I have three copies with me, so you can maybe have it translated soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But does that say essentially what has already been said in the communication before from Dr. Dunjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, he developed it further basically. And just to finish the other topic, the ICMP and I finally established the communication with Mr. Kleiser from the ICMP, and he suggested that he needed to consult the donors of the DNA, family members, which will take, in his view, a couple of weeks, if not months to get. And this really puts us in a very difficult position to do our duty within the time limits allowed by the Trial Chamber. But if I may, I can read out this letter which I can do in a shorter version, which will take me 15 or 20 minutes maybe but you can have a complete picture of the problem, if you want.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps you, first of all, could assist me with some detail. In relation to the DNA testing that has already been done, is the exercise envisaged, looking at the results and the work that was done to achieve these results, and assessing whether that was good or bad or accurate or not, or is the work you envisage actually doing the job again, doing the whole DNA analysis again? Which is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, for the purposes of the motion, I think that, I believe that the analysis that we would like to do is to confirm or let's say put a test to the accuracy of the procedures and proceedings that were collected by the ICMP. But we basic -- our expert told us that he couldn't make any -- he couldn't give us any opinion until he has seen the raw material underlying the aggregate reports made by Dr. Parsons and by others.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But you envisage that it's a question of reviewing the material and the results rather than conducting a totally independent DNA assessment; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't agree with that, because I think that the point he will -- our expert Mr. Stojkovic would like to get his 300 cases of raw material and which includes electropherograms and all the other things that I didn't master, those kind of things, but as I understand it, he -- let me just consult the notes, because I have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation] ... is looking for the material, I am a doctor, I know how these things go, I worked on that, although I am a psychiatrist, but did I cover that in my studies. Anyway, what we need is to have access to all the material available to the experts of the Prosecution when they were compiling their reports. So we need to have exactly the same material that they base their assessment on. We cannot assess their report until we see exactly the same material that they had in front of them when they were drafting their report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That I have clearly understood. It's the purpose that I want to be clear about and it sounds as though the purpose is to review the material, rather than to do a quite separate cross-check. It's a question of looking at what was done and having available all that was before the original expert and coming to a view on the quality of that work. Now, is that your understanding, Mr. Sladojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, my understanding -- I suggested the OTP [indiscernible] a little bit the work of the ICMP in the transcript of Dr. Parson's testimony, and I believe that our experts will want to apply independently the tests on the results of the ICMP which is -- the ICMP changed the methods of extracting the DNA from bones into a more efficient methodology, so basically our expert wants to check whether the results of or a samples taken from bones correspond to the samples given by the DNA donors of the family members, basically, to see whether these correspond. And in order to do that, he needs to have a random sample of 300 cases as suggested, especially in the electronic form because the Prosecution disclosed the electropherograms, which are very important for the analysis in the hard copy format; he cannot do that, because he wants to put the electronic, the electropherograms in his computer system programme and then run the results. And that is only one side of the coin, of the problem, because this is a -- very connected to the work of our pathologist, Dunjic, and conducted both analysis will be able to establish whether the accurate and correct methodology was used in establishing the identity, first of all, of victims, and in addition to that the numbers, and then the reasons and causes or origins of death for the people, for the victims in Srebrenica. As I said, I could read out the shorter version of the letter for you to get a better picture because it really provides the other side of the coin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'll allow you to do that in a moment. Dunjic has already carried out significant amounts of work in connection with other cases, and has given evidence here already. Now, one of these cases is a Srebrenica case and is currently before the Tribunal. I take it that he is able to make use of the work he did in other cases in preparing what he has been asked to do for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: So far the report that is he produced in Srebrenica of course he will be able to use it, but the problem in the Popovic et al case where he also acted as a Defence expert was that he never got the necessary hours to conduct the same analysis that he is suggesting now for our case. That was the problem, and he addresses also among other issue, that issue which occurred in the Popovic et al case, so only to a certain extent he can help us with his analysis in Popovic et al case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And one other thing you mentioned was the problem of consent by relatives to the use of the material. Some correspondence earlier referred to that, but we have not seen a copy of the consent form, do you have that?

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I got the consent form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could I see a copy, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately, it is in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Maybe the Prosecution has a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can show Mr. Sladojevic my copy and I think we probably have the same ones. There were two, Your Honour. If I could show you. I'll hand one to my colleague. [B/C/S on English channel] Your Honour, what we have now is, I suppose I should say just for the record what I'm looking at it's U016-8978 is our evidence number. This is the current form or consent form, Your Honour, which, as I understand it, is -- has been used since 2007. And it's a very clear form where the donor either consents or does not for use in criminal proceedings in courts. The problem is that the vast amount of donors relevant to the Srebrenica case used an earlier form, which I will hand to my colleagues, and Mr. Sladojevic can tell me whether it's the same one. This does not have a number, Your Honour. And the translation is on the top. This one as Dr. Kleiser has explained in his e-mail, which Mr. Sladojevic has shared with us was a short of blanket form which was used by donors, family members, looking for their missing relatives, and does not contemplate use of the samples in national or international courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: If I may, the only thing that we don't understand, and we were never explained, is that our understanding is that some genetic data contains the most private information about the person like the susceptibility to disease or a specific behaviour. And the genes that were and analysed in analysing forensic genetics has specifically been selected. In 1996, it was suggested to us by our expert and so that they can not provide any information with the testing individuals other than their identity. And the only answer that I got about from Mr. Kleiser was that the consent form is self-explanatory. So we have no other information about the suggestion that basically that we don't need to or they don't need to ask for the consents to the donors, although I understand the position is different on your side.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm not sure what that last comment meant, but I'd agree that the consent form is self-explanatory. If I can just say my understanding is that, and I'm not an expert, is that the DNA used or included by the donors may be limited in some respects, but there are still, of course, privacy concerns. It is the person's DNA. It identifies them. And more than that, the entire database which the Defence have requested not only identifies all of the donors, many of whom signed the form stating that their material would be private, but it also, Your Honour, allows one to reconstruct all of the family relationships which can also implicate privacy interest. So it goes beyond just the individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In any event, it's desirable that the use of this material shall be done by agreement. Other the other hand, if reasonable agreement can't be secured, then there is an issue which the Trial Chamber might have to resolve if it was seen that there was some potential unfairness in the use of material which could not be checked, then that would have to be addressed at the appropriate time, and we haven't reached that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, if I may respond to what you've just said. I think there is substantial agreement on many parts of this, which is that the Defence should be able to test the evidence adequately and should have access to it. The only issue is the logistics of obtaining consent properly. Now, what my understanding from the e-mail from Mr. Kleiser, Dr. Kleiser back to the Defence, was that in principle they find the request for 300 samples reasonable. That would entail obtaining consent from around 1.000 individuals, which they will do, but it will take time. The question that hasn't been answered really other than just we need that many is why it needs to be such a large sample, 5 per cent or 300, and why it couldn't start perhaps on a rolling basis with a fewer number of samples. What the Defence have access to, and just to be clear, we don't have any material from ICMP and no in-house material that we are not disclosing. Everything we have from ICMP we have the same as the Defence. But the Defence have, which I've brought a copy of, the missing persons report which is attached, it lists all of the still considered missing from Srebrenica, this is from the ICRC list as well as is identified, as well the periodic updates which we received from ICMP. These updates contain the name of every individual, their date of birth, the case ID, the protocol, lots of information, where they were found, the jurisdiction they were found in, the date of disappearance, the date that the result was submitted or finalised, and the type of report. And this lists, with each update, everybody, every individual identified, and the new individuals are highlighted in a different colour so they can see in a last six months. So there's no reason I can think of why using this list, the Defence couldn't select randomly by year individuals to be tested and ICMP will then obtain the consent forms and as they did regarding Bisina, the Bisina incident in the Popovic case, disclose the entire file. So there's no -- my understanding from the ICMP, there's no refusal to comply. There's no refusal on our part. It's just simply a matter of how to select an adequate representative number, and then, although it will take time, that consent can be obtained and all the information will be provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I assume from all you've said and from the correspondence, Mr. Nicholls, that identity is an essential part of a Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again this is not a part of a case I've worked on, although I was on the Popovic case intimately. What is more important than the identity of the each individual is to show that the persons found are unique individuals. The reason for that is that in some instances parts of one person's body shows up in different sites, different locations as the bodies were moved or shifted around. So more than saying this is so and so, this is this person's name, this is when he was last seen, what is most crucial about the evidence is showing the actual number of unique identified people avoids the problem of perhaps somebody being counted twice. The identifications as well show who these people are, and it is an important part of the case because it shows that they disappeared from Potocari or in the woods, but that evidence is corroborated by lots of -- this has been done before many times and there's -- we feel that is not as crucial as the showing that we've got a unique individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's important not to lose track of the bigger picture here and to remember that the DNA identification of individuals may not be the sole evidence on which the Prosecution is relying, and that the precise determination of the cause of death of individuals may not be something that is essential at the end of the day to prove the broad case that the Prosecution presents. That's not to say that you might not be able to show that perhaps a few cases have been wrongly explained as deaths which look like executions rather than in combat, just to pick an example. Now, I don't dispute for a moment your right to investigate this case in the way you consider appropriate, but when it comes to the use of public resources which have to be authorised, then account has to be taken of the purpose for which this is being done in the context of the case and the issues in the case. At this stage, it's very difficult for me to have a clear picture of how necessary all of this will turn out to be, but what I can tell is that there's agreement that you should be doing the work that you wish to do in relation to a proportion of these examples, and when I say examples, I mean a proportion of all the one who have been identified by this method. But there also seems some sense in what Mr. Nicholls says that while there may be a desirable amount of 300, that there must be a lower starting point at least because it's going to take time to get the necessary authority for whichever number you select here. So I -- what is emerging is consistent with my understanding that -- that you may have been reluctant to commit yourselves to doing things in a certain way because, and I understand your point of view, you might feel well if I say, I'll do 50, then I'll be seen as having given up my case to do 300. Well, I think what is emerging at the moment is that you wouldn't be seen to be doing that because you've got the ICMP on your side as indicating that 300 is a reasonable sample, but I think you are going to have to start this job with a lower number. Bear in mind also this: That at this stage in the case, your concern is with how you challenge 92 ter -- sorry, 92 bis motions, and how you prepare to cross-examine the Prosecution witnesses. There is going to be another stage at which you are going to have to produce reports. Now, I had hoped when all of this started that perhaps your experts would be able to produce reports at this stage in the case. It's clear to me now that that is not going to happen, that it's just impossible, and that we then have to tailor our expectations of the experts. So the main thing is to make sure that you have adequate material for cross-examination, for challenging the Prosecution case. I don't envisage now any agreement being reached that you accept the scientific experts in relation to DNA identification and pathology and exhumation. That's just not going to happen. So you've said what you can so far in respect of that 92 bis motion. If there's anything else -- is the dead-line passed for the -- 1 September. But Mr. Karadzic has already indicated that there's going to be cross-examination of these witnesses, that's his wish. But if there's anything further to be said, then it can be said by the dead-line. But I imagine the Trial Chamber is going to be faced, in this instance, with the question, do we order cross-examination, authorise cross-examination of the evidence in relation to this issue. Now, I can't prejudge that at this stage, but I think without -- I'm sure the Prosecution will understand that indication that it seems likely that some of the Prosecution scientific witnesses included in the motion for eight experts are not likely to be simply accepted by the Trial Chamber without any form of cross-examination. Now, exactly what the decision is will emerge after your submissions have come in. But in relation to this sort of area where there clearly are issues that you are still exploring, and quite rightly exploring, it's difficult to imagine such a decision. Of course the Trial Chamber could postpone the decision and see how your work develops and invite the Prosecution not to lead that evidence until later in the trial and see if there's some issues that can be resolved so that we can then focus, but that's an ongoing exercise. That is not going to be completed in the course of the pre-trial phase. So I would like to hear your comments on the suggestion that ICMP are invited to concentrate on perhaps getting say 100 rather than 300 examples to you to get the work started.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Lordship, I would like to add my comments once Mr. Sladojevic has read a shortened version of the letter by Mr. Dunjic, but in principle, we do agree that complete confidentiality be provided to the donors. And, of course, I don't see why we wouldn't be granted this. But we can't know this until we have all these electropherograms, which we would then use to explore by using a special programme to make sure that there are no duplicates. And as for the consent forms, this could be done once the selection of the 300 random samples has been done, and we can, of course, discuss this with Mr. Stojkovic and Dr. Dunjic to see what the best way to proceed would be. But what I would like to say is we do not oppose certain matters being admitted without cross-examination if they are reasonable and we can confirm that they are accurate. So we are not trying to obstruct anything here, we are just trying to be rational in our procedure. I believe that once we have done our examination and research, and after we have provided our comments, we are sure that the Prosecutor might want to also adapt their own comments and procedure and this could help the economy of the trial. But I would I now like Mr. Sladojevic perhaps to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just one moment. Mr. Nicholls, is it your understanding that [B/C/S on English channel]. Is it your understanding that the electropherograms can be disclosed in electronic form without consent?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. That's not -- excuse me. No, Your Honour, that is not my understanding. I think those were -- the issue I don't understand is why the entire donor database must be disclosed, that's the problem in order for the random selection to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me come back to that. I understand that. Mr. Karadzic, are you saying that the electropherograms themselves do not enable identification of the individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Lordship, now I'm talking about overlaps and duplicates. This is the first task that we need to complete if DNA sample. I'm just talking about the victims and the remains here. If one of the DNA samples is duplicated, we are going to leave it out, so it would be good to look at the entire material without names. At this stage --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's the point I am making. This would enable to you to tell if two samples referred to the one person, I understand that that. Are you saying that that can all be done using material which does not disclose the particular identity, the name of that individual?

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: If I may, Lord Bonomy, we have submitted the request to make available the entire database with DNA profiles and the name of the tested people in order to have the database of the names in advance, so that when our experts sends you a specific request, for specific individual, 300 of them, the parties are certain that the maximum fairness in [Overlapping speakers], but we come to the point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry. We note that the same can be accomplished if the database is presented only with profiles and some unique markers, such as bar-codes without names, and that way the ICMP will protect the information regarding the identity of the victims and their relatives. This is our understanding based on our expert suggestions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls will no doubt respond to that to say, but that still doesn't mean that it can -- you can circumvent the consent form because the consent form is a broader than simply the question of identity. But plainly the purpose of the consent form is to protect either people's concern about identity. But it should be easier, I think, to deal with this issue in the light of this comment. I wonder if the ICMP themselves might not be prepared to take a bold decision about the impact of the consent form in light of a request initially to have material which would not disclose identity.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That may be, Your Honour, and we will consult with ICMP on that. We are meeting with Dr. Kleiser later this week. He is coming here. We hope to meet with him this week and try to resolve all of these issues. In principle and I can't -- I'm not speaking for ICMP, if -- and I don't understand, I have to admit, the exact science of what is saying in the electropherograms, but if there is a way to disclose without identifying the person, I think that that may not be a problem. The initial request was for everything, that is clearly -- would be contrary to the consent forms. And it may be me just not understanding, but what I don't understand is why the initial selection of 100, 200, 300, can't be made off the list and information which they have provided, then once the consent is done --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You are both determined to get to a question I haven't reached yet. I'm quite -- I mean I find this very difficult just as I think Mr. Karadzic seems to be more familiar with it than any of us, but even he has a limited knowledge of the technology involved. I just wanted to be clear, first of all, that one of the requests being made does not involve disclosure of identity. We seem to have established that. The next question is why cannot we find a way of identifying the 300 without disclosing identities of everyone which effectively seems to be what you've asked for to enable that to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: As I understand it, I don't pretend to understand it completely, next to each name there is a probably some unique marker bar-code, numbers, et cetera, if I'm not mistaken. So if the ICMP discloses these database without the names only with these bar-codes that we need to run the test of establishing whether there are repetition of these codes and establishing the exact number of the identified, that would also do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, that would suggest that at least let me explain my understanding of this, that because what is being sought here is indication of duplication, you really need everything, and what is being suggested is that there's a way of providing everything without disclosing identity. Now, that would seem to wrap the two issues together in the way Mr. Sladojevic was trying to do in his earlier submission and you were, to some extent, too. So now we now have a clear understanding, I think, of, well, the layman's understanding of what might be a way of providing sufficient material to make a selection without divulging identity and meanwhile the exercise in obtaining consent could be ongoing, and we might make some progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, just to speaking from what you've said and what my friends have said, if there is a method where it's logistically possible for them to provide information that avoids any problem of duplication and doesn't identify persons or in any way come close to a consent form, I don't see any problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it would -- the purpose wouldn't be to avoid any duplication it would be to establish whether there is any duplication.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's what I'm -- to avoid that problem is what I meant to say, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, if we have reached a suitable stage in the discussion where it appears we've resolved the issue of, as far as we can as lay people, of trying to identify a way of disclosing the necessary material without revealing identities then perhaps now is the time to hear your shortened version of what Dr. Dunjic has written.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can I ask one question. To me it's not clear why there should be -- why you should -- how you should find duplications. If you have a database where you have 5.000 people identified, 5.000 victims identified, how can there be a duplication? If you check random examples of 300 or whatever number, and you find these procedures correct as they were applied, I can't really see how checking the entire database to find duplication ever come up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, if we find that the procedure is accurate then that will be probably our position, but the point is in addition to establishing the identities of persons, I understand that by the way of DNA analysis, you can also establish the time of that. It was suggested to us by our experts. So in addition to identification and making sure there are no duplications in the identification process, then you can also establish the time of that which is also very important, whether it happened in 1992, 1993, 1994, during Srebrenica incidents or later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think there have also in the Tribunal been examples of fairly closely related family members being identified by DNA, but there being uncertainty about who was there, and yet there have been duplicate and triplicate identifications of people. It is a possibility. I'm not suggesting that that is necessarily the issue here. But for present purposes, I'm prepared to accept that the Defence experts have a genuine concern to establish something that would either reassure them or give them a basis for further investigation, and it seems to me that we are beginning to get to a point where can be done within realistic period of time and extent of time, which is the issue that obviously concerns those who provide the funds.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I ask one related question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: If Dr. Stojkovic had his 300 complete case files now, how long would that take? How long would he need to analyse those 300 and come up with his results?

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I believe, if not mistaken, that we requested 450 hours or 300 hours for Mr. Stojkovic. Do you remember that, Ms. Reinhardt?

utterances.speaker: MS. REINHARDT
utterances.text: Yes, you have requested 150 to 300 hours for Mr. Stojkovic and about 800 hours for Mr. Dunjic at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't propose to go anywhere on this particular subject with OLAD because it's impossible to say anything definite about the issue on the material that we've been discussing. That may change depending on what emerges from your initial exploration of the data, which I hope you now get. So let's lay that aside and let's move to the Dunjic issue and can I hear from you the abbreviated form of the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Lord Bonomy, we already found ourselves in the vicious circle because of the hours necessary but we will come to that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah, but you are not going to be able to put forward a sustainable argument about hours unless you start doing some work and demonstrate something solid to justify not just exceptional but highly exceptional measure that you are requesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: May I read it in Serbian language so the interpreters can translate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I'll try to be as short as possible. [Interpretation] Over the last four years I have been working in processing the various locations relating to Srebrenica in the case of Vujadin Popovic and the rest. We --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. -- just hold on, you'll be able to read it much more quickly if there's a copy you can give to the interpreter. But even then you have to allow for the problem of probably technical language in there. And please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: On the reports, the reports of the Prosecution experts, Richard Wright; Fredy Peccerelli; Christopher Lawrence; Haglund, William; John Clark; and Jose Pablo Baraybar represent collective reports of the localities with comments of their findings. In order to evaluate and comments their reports, I had to look at the autopsy reports related to the sites in question. In that way, I analysed their collective reports and their specific conclusions, primarily that of Haglund, Clark, and Baraybar, and I made numerous objections or remarks. And I indicated the inconsistencies between the general conclusions and the autopsy reports, especially in terms of the cause of death and the mechanism of injury, the localities of Sandici and Potocari and Vesinje [as interpreted] were processed by the local pathologist of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the supervision of the ICTY. In the analysis of their reports, I found numerous failings and inconsistencies between the findings and the conclusions on the cause of death. The reason for the inconsistency between the pathology reports and the concluded cause of death of the pathologists who did the autopsies and the main pathologists who made the collective report in their expert reports, I also said that the reason for this is in the data by Haglund on page 11 of his reports for task of June 15th, 1998. The autopsy of the victims began on the 31st of July, 1996, and lasted until the 22nd of August, 1996. The autopsies were carried out in temporary morgues in the war damaged factory of -- textile factory in the outskirts of Kalesija. The autopsies were conducted under the supervision of Dr. Robert Kirschner, the director of international forensic programme of the organisation, Doctors for Human Rights. In the establishment of their final conclusion on the cause and matter of death, as well as in the editing of the final version of the autopsy reports, the legal advisor of ICTY, Peter McCloskey, assisted a summary of the pathological findings was written by Dr. Page Hudson [phoen]. Last year, Dr. Dunjic presented to the Court, and Mr. McCloskey objected quite dramatically to this. The problem presented and noted by Mr. Dunjic was that in the lists of the ICMP and the International Red Cross persons as missing throughout that whole report in relation to Srebrenica, names of persons are mentioned who were exhumed at specific locations and for whom there is evidence that they died before the 11th of July, 1995, and some of them substantially after the 1st of October, 1995. According to information from the cited documents, it arises that the victims of genocide in Srebrenica among those are also identified remains of individuals who disappeared in 1993, and those who disappeared after 30th of July, 1995. In the case file of the Prosecution of the cantonal court in Tuzla, it is stated that the cemetery or the grave of Blijcevac [phoen] contained bodies that had nothing to do with the fall of Srebrenica. Thirty-nine bodies were found there. In relation to this, it is important to analyse two documents, the first one is the report by Mr. Janc, and the second one is a list, ERN 0663290, examples of identified persons from the list of the Prosecution and the database of the B & H Army only for cases of those killed and missing soldiers before July 1995, which was given by Mr. Geoffrey Nice. There is a correction by the ICTY which is -- has to do --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I am afraid we are finding it a little bit difficult because you are not reading in order, so we cannot exactly -- and it's very fast. Yes, but we need to know where you are reading from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you assist by when you move, missing out something, just indicate so that the interpreter can find the part.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I will do so. Apologies to the interpreters [Interpretation] We are now on page 3 paragraphs 2 and 3: Dusan Janc, investigator of the Prosecution made a clarification in order to correct identification that refers to Kravica and Branjevo as locations of executions and identified persons at those places of execution. As far as the executions in Kravica, at the moment all identified persons a total of 1.319 cannot be linked with this place of execution. The conclusion is based on different sources including expert report, documents, statement by witnesses and their testimony. And then on the same page under B: Examples of identified persons from the list of the Prosecution and the database of the B & H Army where a specific number of persons are referred to for which the Army of the B & H and the command says were killed in 1992, 1993, and 1994 as cases of members of the B & H Army who were killed up to July 1995 and whose remains were found and identified in various graves which are then referred to. On page 4: In the cited report and all the reports of the ICMP, the International Red Cross and the institute for missing persons investigated so far, different dates are given for death of the same identified person. Dr. Dunjic doesn't know how this was established. In the mentioned list, a large number of persons from the list of the B & H Army, there are two different dates of death for a large number of persons and they are very different. This difference can and must be established by looking at the autopsy reports and the forensic expert reports. The document provided by the command of the B & H Army also contains these discrepancies, so the question is: What is the exact date of death and based on what information it is established? It is possible to responds to this question only on the basis of forensic findings of the found remains, the state of the bodies, the decomposition of the bodies found, and the skeletal remains, and compare that with the documents and statements of other people. And as far as the Sandici and Potocari locations are concerned, it has been established that there is a different degree of putrification, changes, and skeletisation, partial or complete mummification in bodies, which indicates the conclusion that these are cases of bodies buried at different times. For all the above, I believe that we need to insist on an analysis of specific locations, specifically those from Eastern Bosnia. The aim of the forensic analysis was to compare the methodology of the autopsies after 2002, used by experts of the ICTY, their findings, and also to carry out an analysis of the age of the bodies and compare that with the age of the bodies on which the Tribunal investigators worked until 2001. The age of the bodies, the change, in an indirect way indicates that certain mass graves were filled on several locations and not all bodies from the mass graves are linked with the events in Srebrenica. For this analysis we need to check their identification, the DNA identification, because you can also establish the time of death by looking at the lists of those identified. The third thing that I am suggesting actually one of the conclusion that I had in analysing previous locations that refers to the mechanism of injury is that there is no in-depth analysis of the injuries and possible manner of injury, and this is important because in the compiled reports of the experts of the Prosecution, a large number of bodies found indirectly indicate that they had been shot or that they were executed from the autopsy findings. This is impossible to establish in the largest number of cases so that it can only be assumed how the persons died. This also offers ample opportunity for manipulation. For a certain number of cases, from all localities, I have established that they could have been killed in direct fighting. The injuries from shells, projectiles of large calibre and of great force, PAMs, Zoljas, and so on were numerous in various localities, and this can also be checked from witness statements from many parts in various periods. On page 7, Dr. Dunjic also says that: There is a description of events of July 1995, the manner that brigades of the BH Army were formed in Srebrenica, the participation of witnesses in them, their breakthroughs through Republika Srpska army formations, their capturing, as well as the description of the conflicts and the death of a large number of people in this period. A joint conclusion which can be concluded from all of the above are following and this can be very useful: One, a lot of the victims were killed in direct battles; two, the localities, the victims were killed in various localities around Srebrenica; three, most men were members of the BH Army; four, the wounding and killing was performed by various artillery means.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Sladojevic please slow down. I'm still at number 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you go back to number four and just read a bit more slowly again, Mr. Sladojevic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I will did so. [Interpretation] Four, the wounding and killing was inflicted by various artillery pieces; five, some bodies of the victims had already been skeletonised in that period; six, women, children, and elderly were evacuated from Srebrenica before the conflict; seven, a certain number of BH Army soldiers was captured; eight, some captured individuals died in camps as a result of previous wounding or famine; nine, some prisoners were tied up and later questioned; and ten, many of the captured soldiers were physically and psychologically abused. The witness statements also offer a number of issue that can be analysed, concluded based on the analysis of autopsy reports: The time of death, the manner of death, whether all the killings were -- all the deaths were in the same location or not, which can also be determined on the base of their wounding, among other things. Whether among the victims there were also those who had died in any manner before or after the critical period between the 11th and 19th July, 1995, and in order to answer all these questions, it is necessary to compare autopsy reports and DNA analysis of all of the identified individuals from this area. In the Popovic case, there were -- there is a list of folders that were never analysed because not enough time was assigned for this, and he insisted he needs additional time, and also information that could be found in various other DVDs which were subsequently provided to him by us. And soon we will come to his opinion on page 8, paragraph -- the last paragraph. Dr. Dunjic mentions that there are inconsistencies in the aggregate reports of these experts of the Prosecution, and that these inconsistencies can only be established on the basis of an analysis of the aggregate reports and autopsy reports on which they were founded. These inconsistencies were -- I point out in my expertise of the expert reports of the Prosecution, however, on the basis of the documents that we provided to him, I have pointed out some localities in Eastern Bosnia which were analysed by experts and commissions of the Federation of BH, and we believe that this might be significant to re-analyse these because from these documents we can see further inconsistencies in the findings and the conclusions as to the cause of death. In addition, the changes on the bodies that are mentioned in the reports point to the different times of death and burying, and I felt that the additional hour that is I would be -- that the hour that is I was given for or granted to report this were insufficient and I would need an additional 120 hours which would be a minimum in order to analyse the autopsy reports and the exhumation reports and the following documentation. At the end of his letter, Dr. Dunjic also offers his own opinion, which consists of several portions. Under one, he discusses the cause of death saying that the cause of death on decomposed bodies cannot be established with certainty and it can be -- they can be understood only very conditionally. And all pathologists and even anthropologists are decisive in their conclusions regarding the perimortem injuries and the injuries that were -- that came about after their death. Generally speaking, in their joint reports there are two major issues. First of all they all speak of in life changes, in manners that point to the fact that it is impossible to determine the cause of death on skeletonised bodies after their death. All the experts, forensic experts, adopt the assumption, and I reiterate, the assumption that these injuries by fire-arms were inflicted during their life. In their reports, all these experts say that this is a doctrine that is accepted, however this doctrine is not accepted by this profession. However, in addition to these data and the data provided by Mr. Haglund, based on autopsy reports of victims which started on 31st July and went on until August 22nd, he said that all these deaths were inflicted in the area of Kalesija and he also says that in doing these reports, and examinations, he was assisted by a Prosecutor, Mr. McCloskey. This is unacceptable as far as the profession is concerned. In addition, the injuries that were determined to have been done by a blunt instrument and which are considered to have been inflicted while the victim is alive, is not something that is taken as a position on which to base their conclusion that such injuries were actually inflicted after death. It is impossible to determine whether such injuries were actually inflicted during battle or in some other manner.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Sladojevic please slow down a little bit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sladojevic, another request to slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where are we, can we go back to a suitable --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Pilica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The additional injuries, gun-shot wounds to the heads of a number of victims, point to a conclusion that fire was opened from immediate or absolute vicinity. Such a conclusion does not comply with the forensic doctrine and autopsy reports because it is impossible to establish, among others, the sequence of the injuries in addition to the fact that these were decomposed bodies. And I consider that it would be very useful if the doctors who performed the autopsies and prepared these aggregate reports used the international classifications of injuries and wounds as mentioned below and then I will skip this part, but he also says that: I also consider that it is necessary, before the Court, to determine the consequences under which the death was inflicted. In order to be of assistance to the Court, the doctors could determine precise and complete reports and prepare precise and complete reports for every individual and only then would it be possible to establish facts for a group of individuals from a certain location either exhumed or on whom the autopsy was performed. This is precisely the reason why I insist that it is necessary to examine each body and each body part to determine the entries. In his report, Dr. Lawrence among other things, says the following: There were many skull injuries, rib injuries, and hip injuries which were deliberately inflicted after death in order to obscure the injuries to those parts of the bodies which were inflicted while the victim was alive. The intent is something that is to be determined by a Court in any legal system. However, as an expert who provides a report, this person is not professionally -- is not professional enough to provide this kind of opinion and to discuss intent. Under item 14 of the same document it says that: In the case of six bodies, the cause of death was impossible to determine, and the conclusion was that they were probably -- they probably had perforating wounds of soft tissues which were inflicted by a fire-arm. However, it is impossible to determine that or see that because there was loss of soft tissues due to decomposition changes. This type of opinion is not based on the professional standards and it can cause significant damage to the -- to the work that they produce. There is not a single report, a single full report for one particular locality that would encompass all the cases beginning with the description of the location, the transport, the traces, exhumations, photo documents, and identification. Opinion number 3 relates to the mechanism of injuries which was not established, and there was no in-depth analysis of the injuries and the possible ways that they were inflicted. Based on the autopsy reports provided, it is impossible to determine this in most of the cases so that we can only assume the manner of death of the individuals. In addition to shells and large calibre projectiles, and similar, which can be found in numerous localities, it can be concluded with some truthfulness that a large number of deaths, the autopsied bodies were actually killed during combat in the period mentioned above. The joint conclusions are the following: First, a large number of the victims died in combat; number two, the victims around numerous locations were found around Srebrenica; three, most men were members of the BH Army; four, there were wounded by various and killed by various artillery assets; five, some bodies were already skeletonised in the period, in review; six, women, children, and elderly persons had been evacuated from Srebrenica before the conflict; seven, a certain number of BH Army soldiers were captured; eight, some individuals died in camps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sladojevic, it's repetition now, is there anything else of substance to be added?

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: There is. We are approaching the end. [Interpretation] The fourth opinion put forth by Dr. Dunjic is that: Based on the review of the work of the pathologists, we can conclude that in the case of Nova Kasaba, Ravnice, and Zeleni Jadar as well as Pilica their work was very shoddy. They did not produce autopsy reports that could later be analysed and surveilled so that relevant information could be drawn from them. In their conclusions, they proceeded from assumptions that all the injuries were inflicted perimortem, which means during the life of the victim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I've heard enough for today's purposes. I'm beginning to suspect that this might even be a way of reading some of the Defence case into a document which is going to be made public and that's not the purpose of today's hearing. The meeting today is to look at ways of resolving issues. Now, you've advanced a number of arguments by Dr. Dunjic. I'm not clear if he is the only person whose opinion is being expressed there, because at one stage you talked about joint conclusions. Are we confine -- is this letter confined to his own opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: This is only for his own [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, is there any other specific additional argument to be made because you'll appreciate many of these points relate to evidence which is available whether you do a DNA analysis or a postmortem analysis, and the post mortem analysis is perhaps an additional confirmation; but there already is, according to him, evidence to support the points that he is making without further expert examination. Now, is there any other point beyond that to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I can only summarise the point Mr. Dunjic is making which is that [Interpretation] This is page 15 now of the letter and it is somewhere in the middle of the page where it begins: However, from all the analysed cases, it's not possible to establish the precise cause of death because of skeletonisation and putrefaction, it's not possible to establish the time of death or the mechanism of injury because the given descriptions in the autopsy findings do not correspond to the collective report by Mr. Haglund which he gave, especially to his comments and interpretation, Nova Kasaba and Pilica. Certain number of injuries at all the locations of Nova Kasaba, Pilica, Zeleni Jadar and Ravnice indicates that it's possible that individuals were injured in combat. There were statements by witnesses and in order to establish the cause of death of from other locations and based on 3.221 cases, I need to be allowed additional work time of 500 hours. Sincerely yours, Mr. Dunjic. [In English] Especially bearing in mind the Prosecution had 15 years at its disposal to make the same conclusions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, your last point from the letter about the hours is obviously a crucial part of this. In an earlier part of that letter there was reference to an additional 120 hours. What is the relationship between these two figures?

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: The OLAD has authorised so far 120 additional hours for our forensic expert, for the handwriting expert for Mr. Stojkovic and for Mr. Dunjic. And it was basically left up to us to decide how we are going to allocate those hours and we decided that since Dr. Dunjic is dealing with six OTP experts that he should take all 120 hours because the amount of material that he needs to go through is very voluminous. Whereas, since we are still in the process of obtaining documents from the ICMP, there is not much that Dr. Stojkovic can do until we received documents from the ICMP, so he can start his analysis as well. But the main problem is that Dr. Stojkovic will not be able to start the analysis until he has been authorised additional hours to perform the analysis that he needs to do. And that's why we say we are in the vicious circle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are lawyers the only professionals in the world who work pro bono.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, do we need to comment on that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was that letter -- is that letter addressed to OLAD?

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: That was written for the purpose of this meeting so that the Trial Chamber and the Prosecution and the OLAD gets the overall picture of the problem that we would like to analysis as well to do and to perform. That is basically our duty. But we would like also to hear from the OLAD because we simply fail to understand the -- it was suggested by the OLAD that we should do a certain kind of analysis and that we will be allowed later to perform a more detailed analysis, but we fail to understand why don't we just resolve this matter while it's now on the agenda? We could resolve everything now and then there is no need later to ask for additional hours for expertise, et cetera, because it's already on the agenda. We didn't want to do this analysis in the first place. It was the idea of the Prosecution. We need to respond, and we need to respond adequately and properly. And we don't believe that OLAD is in a position to know better what our expert needs to do. And as I said, Dr. Dunjic never suggested that he would examine the entirety of the role information underlying the reports, but as you said four or five months of full-time work or approximately two so many Euros, we are trying to find a solution, but it's very hard when the Prosecution tendered a very voluminous material that we need to go through. There is no reason that we should just run a superficial analysis and then only to later run another analysis which would be thorough analysis. I fail to understand why don't we just resolve this issue now while it's being on the agenda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But do I correctly understand that what he has in mind is analysing every postmortem report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No, he doesn't, because that's physically not possible. So he suggested that within those 120 hours currently authorised that he would analyse 30 to 40 per cent of the material disclosed randomly selected by him in order to come to certain conclusions. But the main problem with the hours authorised is that our experts are not in a position to give us any opinion because in order to give us an opinion, they need to have additional necessary hours to perform analysis. Once they perform analysis they will come up with an opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I am sorry, I haven't understood that correctly. You are saying that he suggested using 120 additional hours to review 30 to 40 per cent of the postmortem materials; is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: That's been disclosed to us in the past month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Now, can I take it then that the 500 hours was with a view to analysing every postmortem report?

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't believe that he meant the entire raw material database, but in relation to also to other -- basically to all the grave sites in Eastern Bosnia. That's what I understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, he still has these 120 hours in hand, does he? He hasn't used them yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: He used around 30 hours because he needed to go through the material in order to write this kind of a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was that not an earlier 30 hours --

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Part of this 120. But he is saying to you that he can carry out a review of 30 to 40 per cent on the 120 hour basis; is that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, he will probably be able to produce an opinion by mid-September or towards the end of September.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that will be based on establishing or confirming some of the points he has made in that list of criticisms of the OTP material.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes indeed. Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Don't you think that's adequate for the purposes of the preparing to deal with the Prosecution case?

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: I believe it's up to Dr. Karadzic to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You are quite right, it's not a question for you, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: Merely I can say that my understanding is that we could -- maybe we could -- it is important to establish the causes, et cetera, of that because in the end it is -- it directly relates to the qualification of the crime committed -- allegedly crime commited in Srebrenica, whether it was a genocide or war crime against war prisoners, et cetera, but it's really up to Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Lordship, with all due respect to all present at this meeting I have the impression that Defence cases do not bear the same weight and the conviction if as when something it missed from the Prosecution case, this is not done in a convincing way, that some allegations do not stand. So I hear of the idea that we need to establish the complete accuracy of the Prosecution case and then our job in the Defence would be much easier. What we have here is a false picture where the number of illegally killed has been magnified or augmented by ten. In Bosnia, now they are talking about 10.000 victims even 20.000 victims, so leaving aside the fact that any illegal death does not go to the credit of anyone, and those persons should be held responsible before the law, and this is up to us, not to our opponents. But in order for this area to have a future, for purposes of the future of Balkans and as whole and the future of Europe, it is very importance to establish precisely what happened. And in the Defence case, this will not be possible if we fail to look at this massive date which are going to be presented, and we have to provide our counterevidence and convincing arguments in the face of such a vast amount of detail that would be provided by the Prosecution. Already we are in the position, and we can see that we will be in the position to be able to present completely to the Chamber of how what has been presented to it so far actually looks like in the light of what actually happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will find though that in the course of the Prosecution case a realistic cross-examination is going to be selective. It's going to prioritise, and its going to take examples of the type that are set out in Dr. Dunjic's letter. And its going to rely on the inconsistency between other evidence about death of people and what is said in the reports and so on. The cross-examination in the Prosecution case is not going to go through every one of these deaths and analyse it with each expert witness. So the issue for OLAD isn't quite the one that you are identifying at the moment. Maybe by the end of the case the issue is the one that you've just identified, but at this stage it may not be. And that is traditionally been the way that things have operate here, that there's been an allocation of expert hours to enable you to deal adequately with the Prosecution case and then other allocation to deal preparation of any report that is follow. And obviously the success you have with the Prosecution case may have a significant bearing on the allocation of the hours, if you still seek additional hours at that stage, for the provision of your final report for the presentation of your own Defence case. Now, I understand your anxiety about trying to do it all now, and I understand that you may well have an argument that that is a more efficient way of doing it, but the question is who is to determine that, and I think in the first instance it's a matter for OLAD to assess and decide whether the right way to deal with this is the traditional way or whether you've said enough to justify and even further exceptional arrangement. You've presented a very full statement and account of the position. I think that letter should be translated as quickly as possible by -- and I don't know who is going to undertake that offhand but it should be done as quickly as possible and then communicated to OLAD along with whatever covering letter you wish to submit. But I suggest, Dr. Karadzic, that you do give thought to whether non-compromise of any kind is the answer to this particular issue. And whether Dr. Dunjic cannot do a perfectly adequate job for present purposes on the basis of the hours already allocated and the arguments that he has presented with an analysis of 30 to 40 per cent of the postmortem material. Anyway, that's a matter for the parties to think about. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand that what I was saying referred only to OLAD. What I wanted to emphasise was that Dunjic is working on the evidence of six Prosecution experts. So he needs to do that with his associates. It's not possible for him to do that. On the other hand, what I wanted to say is that OLAD, well, I believe that I am very cooperative out of respect for all the people involved, and OLAD would need to be sensitive about the importance of the whole case, and never mind equality of arms. The six OTP experts had the time and the hour that is they had, so we need to establish an adequate proportion of time for the Defence experts for them to come out something that will actually be a true opposition of arguments or confrontation of arguments, not something that is just superficial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: They were, of course, doing a rather different job from the one that arises now. It's one of the features of this Tribunal and some might be critical of it, that it is essentially adversarial in nature. However, experts truly doing the job that they are professional expertise is dedicated to are not protagonists of one side or the other, unless some attack -- unless some attack can be made on their impartiality as experts, then they can be viewed as independent professionals carrying out an exercise for which their own self-respect as professional experts is answerable. Now, there has been -- well, there have been and are experts who are engaged by the Prosecution. They may be engaged in different ways, but the professionals we are talking about in the scientific arena are on the face of it, of what we read, independent experts doing a job as part of an international effort to investigate these events. So it would be wrong to look at every element of this as a adversarial presentation. That is not to say the Prosecution might not tend to put their own interpretation and gloss, the best one that they can perhaps present in support of their case on the material, but when we are looking, as we are at the moment, on the basic -- at the basic material itself, before I would be prepared to view an expert as other than working impartially in the interest of justice, I would have to see some basis for doing so. So what I'm more concerned about in the light of all that's been said today is the indication given by Professor Dunjic that he sees bases for criticising the way in which the job has been done, the results that have been achieved, and the interpretation of these results. And he is not suggesting that people have been doing this in a biased and partial way. He is suggesting that it's not perhaps the way it ought to have been done and that he, as an expert, takes a different view. Well, that's legitimate position to be taken, even in your legal system, I think, where the expert would essentially be a court-engaged expert. But there may be circumstances in which he can be challenged. And that's the sort of area that, it seems to me, is in issue here. Now, that doesn't mean that you go back to square one and do the job completely again. It means that you dip sample the work of the experts. You demonstrate legitimate criticisms, then you try to justify on the basis of that, securing, if necessary, more hours to complete the job. But it seems to me that OLAD's exceptional allocation in this case has given you a pretty good basis for carrying out a fair assessment of a large proportion of the postmortem material. I can see circumstances in which that could lead to you presenting an argument for yet more, but whether Dr. Dunjic needs to insist on a complete analysis of all the material, I think it's questionable. Now, I am expressing only my own personal reaction here with a view to encouraging you with OLAD to reach an agreement that will allow you sufficient scope to deal with the 92 bis motion if you wish to say any more on it, and to challenge -- prepare to challenge the Prosecution case, on the understanding that his final report will be prepared on the basis of a further allocation at the time of the Defence case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: If I may, we are very anxious that should we fail in conducting a proper analysis of the OTP proposed or preferred forensic expert evidence, that there is a possibility at least that the Trial Chamber will accept the reports, and that we will not get the opportunity to cross-examine the experts, and then it will have to deal with it later in our Defence case, which is completely different from our proposition that we are entitled to cross-examine or Dr. Karadzic. And in order to do that, we have to convince the Trial Chamber that we are entitled to do so. And in order to be able to convince the Trial Chamber that we are entitled to do so, we need to perform a thorough analysis and come up with strong arguments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You may find that there would be some value for the Chamber in you making a submission based on the letter which you've read out today and selecting the appropriate elements that are demonstrated in that, as long as you've got a material basis to support what Dunjic is saying. He is giving you conclusions without telling you the precise source of his conclusions, at least in some instances. And it may be that you need to supplement what is in that as part of your submission. But that is obviously material which you can use to support an argument that Dr. Karadzic should be entitled to cross-examine these experts. As I said earlier, I've abandoned hope of reaching agreement on this area, and it would be silly, I think, to try to press that any further. Now, the Prosecution have been silent because we haven't really given them a chance to say anything recently, but maybe there is nothing to be added.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The only -- my only observation would be having heard now what Dr. Dunjic is writing, you are actually already in a position to make a response to the 92 bis evidence of some of the experts that he refers to, and I would say you have made the points that would actually lead to cross-examination. So that's all I can say. So he needs only 30 hours basically to solve the question that -- which is currently on the table.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And just for the avoidance of any doubt, we've been talking about these 120 hours, but I think -- is that the additional allocation that applies to all three witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. REINHARDT
utterances.text: If I may just very quickly explain that. We have already on one hand we have doubled the pre-trial allotment to 300 hours all together for all the experts that we are going to assign in the pre-trial phase, which is more than the three. For mainly in order to prepare reports because that's what usually is done. That's what we can do under our remuneration scheme is to allocate hours for the production of expert reports. Usually we wouldn't even be in a position to allocate money for the review of material for experts without the outcome of a report afterwards. So in this case, we have in addition to these 300 hours allocated another 120 hours for these three experts which also included Lacroix at the time, but mainly Dunjic and Stojkovic to go through the materials and basically come up with what is in this letter. That was our understanding at the time that for now they just needed to respond to the OTP motion and indicate whether cross-examination is necessary in the point of view of the Defence or not. And in our opinion, that was basically what we thought was the purpose of these 120 hours. That doesn't mean that if it comes out, as already obviously did for Mr. Dunjic, that there needs to be further challenge of the OTP experts and that he might actually want to come up with a report, he obviously can use some of the 300 hour that are still in the pot, and as we have already talked with Mr. Robinson, I understand, we also offered the possibility to take hours from the allotment for the trial phase, which is, again, two times 150 hour, 150 for OTP phase and 150 for the Defence phase to be able to pull that forward basically to the pre-trial phase. If the argument the Defence is we don't want to wait until the Defence phase to come out with reports on other own behalf but we want to do it all now, we offered the possibility to do that, but I understand that that was actually not accepted by the Defence team and they said they don't want to do this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's something obviously that Dr. Karadzic can think about again, but what is emerging from this is that you have the best -- most of your more or less 100 hours on hand in this particular area, but you've got three experts that that relates to. If you use them all on Dunjic, obviously you may suffer consequences in relation to the others, but it doesn't sound as though you really do need to use all of these hours on Dunjic. I agree with you that Dunjic should do more and do some analysis of a significant proportion of the postmortem report toss back up the points he is making so that he is presenting Dr. Karadzic with a report which will give him a sound basis for cross-examining the Prosecution experts in the Prosecution phase of the case. But it may be that you are able to keep and reserve all that may be available to you for the Defence phase because you may want to work on presentation of a case using the lessons that are learned from the success or otherwise of the cross-examination. That's a question of judgement. If you don't want to do that, if you want to make use of all the hours now, then the offer is being made that some of these, at least, can be advanced to this stage and used at this stage of the case. If you feel that would enable you then to make a better presentation in challenging the OTP and then in also presenting your Defence case, then that's a matter for your judgement. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Lordship, before the Prosecution case, my primary concern is that maybe because of an insufficient number of hours that we are allocated, we will fail to be persuasive enough before the Trial Chamber. If that should happen, that error is incorrigible later on because I cannot really claim that the Trial Chamber has reached a decision without proper, without due examination, if I fail to present sufficient evidence for them to make another decision. Now, further, we need to actually clarify and point out and highlight the arguments that the Prosecution is offering. So I need to have a sufficient number of hours in order to actually persuade the Trial Chamber to rule in my favour, to security my right to cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I think we've exhausted this particular subject. As I indicated at the beginning, it's not for me to make decisions on this, I can only try to facilitate agreement that's going to enable everyone to have a fair opportunity to present their respective cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Perhaps one point, we would appreciate if the decision on the 92 bis motion for the expert would be postponed to a later date until everything is ready, and I also can say that the Srebrenica part of the case will definitely not -- will definitely be at the end of the Prosecution case, so there's no need to have it all ready by the beginning of the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not inclined to postpone the decision on this at my own hand. If it was left to me, I would want this decision made fairly soon, partly for the reasons that Dr. Karadzic himself has advanced, that it will be of assistance to know the position. It's, what, another two weeks before this response is due. I think the response should come in. The Trial Chamber will be alerted to what you've said and we'll consider whether the decision ought to be made then. I will write a brief note summarising this discussion so that emphasis is placed on the most important parts of this discussion, and it will then be for the Trial Chamber at the appropriate stage, which could be in September, to make their decision. If they decide to postpone it, then whether they would notify you or simply wait until an appropriate time, I don't know, and I don't think it really helps very much for there to be this uncertainty.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I was actually only think being the DNA, not about Dunjic, just the DNA, not the other experts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, I can see the value in relation to the DNA expert. Yes. Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I owe an explanation here. It is not our position that these experts should be questioned, that their expertise should be questioned, that they have deliberately misled anyone.
